readingInstruction: Read Revelation 17:1-18:24. Two chapters describe the fall of Babylon the great, first as a prostitute riding a beast, then as a great city mourned by merchants and kings. Notice the contrast between Babylon and the Bride of the Lamb, who appears in chapter 19.
settingTheScene: In the Old Testament, Babylon was the empire that destroyed Jerusalem and took Israel into exile, and it became the symbol of human pride and opposition to God, from the tower of Babel (Genesis 11) onward. In the first century, Babylon was a code name for Rome, the city on seven hills that dominated the Mediterranean world. In Revelation, Babylon is both of these and more: the world system organized against God, seductive, wealthy, and violent, in every age. The prophets Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel used a similar language for the cities of Babylon and Tyre. John’s readers would hear the echoes.
observation: “And I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast that was full of blasphemous names” (17:3).
“I saw the woman, drunk with the blood of the saints, the blood of the martyrs of Jesus” (17:6).
“They will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings” (17:14).
“Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues” (18:4).
“I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see” (18:7).
“Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her!” (18:20).
interpretation:
One of the seven angels with the bowls invites John to see “the judgment of the great prostitute who is seated on many waters, with whom the kings of the earth have committed immorality.” In the Spirit, John sees a woman sitting on a scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns, dressed in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold, jewels, and pearls, holding a golden cup full of abominations. On her forehead is a name of mystery: “Babylon the great, mother of prostitutes and of earth’s abominations.” She is “drunk with the blood of the saints, the blood of the martyrs of Jesus.” John marvels greatly, and the angel explains the mystery. The beast “was, and is not, and is to come” (a parody of God’s “who is and who was and who is to come”). The seven heads are seven mountains (an allusion to Rome’s seven hills) and also seven kings. The ten horns are ten kings who receive authority for a brief time. They give their power to the beast and “will make war on the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are called and chosen and faithful.” The woman “is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth.” Interpreters debate the exact historical identification of the kings, but the point is that every earthly power that opposes Christ is doomed. And, strikingly, the beast and the ten kings turn on the prostitute and destroy her: evil devours itself.

In chapter 18, the scene shifts to the city’s fall. An angel with great authority lights up the earth: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a dwelling place for demons, a haunt for every unclean spirit.” The reason is that all nations have drunk of the wine of her immorality, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxurious living. Then a voice from heaven calls God’s people: “Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues.” It is a call to separation. Believers are to live in the world without being of it, refusing its idolatries and injustices, and ready to leave if loyalty to Christ requires it. The prophets said the same of the ancient Babylon (Jeremiah 51:45).

The woman’s self-image is: “I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see.” Because of her pride, “in a single day her plagues will come, death and mourning and famine, and she will be burned up with fire.” The kings of the earth, merchants, and shipmasters mourn her: “Alas! Alas! You great city.” The merchants weep because “no one buys their cargo anymore.” The cargo list is long: gold, silver, jewels, fine linen, spices, wine, grain, cattle, horses and chariots, “and slaves, that is, human souls.” The final item reveals the system’s true cost: human lives sold as commodities. The empire’s wealth was built on trafficking in people. Their grief is not for her but for their profits.

Heaven, however, responds with joy: “Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her!” A mighty angel throws a stone like a great millstone into the sea: “So will Babylon the great city be thrown down with violence, and will be found no more.” The sounds of harpists, musicians, craftsmen, millstones, lamps, and brides and grooms will cease. “And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints, and of all who have been slain on earth.” All injustice is judged. The city of man is overthrown to make room for the city of God.
connection: Genesis 10-11 introduces Babel and Babylon. Isaiah 13-14, 21:9, 47, Jeremiah 50-51, and Daniel 4:30 describe ancient Babylon’s pride and fall. Ezekiel 26-28 describes the fall of Tyre. Nahum 3:4 uses prostitution for a city. Hosea 2 and Jeremiah 3 use prostitution for unfaithfulness. 2 Corinthians 6:14-18 and 1 John 2:15-17 call for separation from the world. Isaiah 52:11 and Jeremiah 51:6, 45 say “come out.” Ezekiel 27 lists the merchants of Tyre. Amos 8:4-6 and James 5:1-6 condemn exploiting the poor. 1 Peter 5:13 uses Babylon for Rome.
application:
Ask where you are drawn by the glamor and luxury of Babylon. What do you envy or chase that the world offers?

Consider the supply chains and systems you depend on. Ask whether any of them are built on the exploitation of people, and what you can do about it.

Pray for believers living in places of persecution and temptation, that they would be kept faithful.
prayerPrompts: Worship Jesus as Lord of lords and King of kings.
Thank him that Babylon has fallen and he has won.
Ask him to help you come out of whatever you are entangled with.
